article._excerpt: Award-winning documentary on 2018 northern B.C. wildfires coming to Williams Lake | Williams Lake Tribune Award-winning documentary on 2018 northern B.C. wildfires coming to Williams Lake The Fire In Our Hearts, an award-winning wildfire documentary, is coming to Williams Lake on Nov. 7 and Nov. 12 at Paradise CInemas. As wildfires raged in 2018 forcing his friends, family and neighbours to choose to evacuate or remain to protect the land that defines them filmmaker Josias Tschanz knew he wanted to give his remote community in northern B.C. a voice. Tschanz is bringing his feature length award-winning documentary that he hopes will spark discussion, The Fire In Our Hearts, to Williams Lake on Saturday, Nov. 7 and Thursday, Nov. 12. The film follows communities located directly south of Francois Lake and tells the story of ordinary residents, First Nations and firefighters who chose flight over flight.. “At first it was not a film,” Tschanz said noting, he immigrated to Canada when he was 16 years old from Switzerland and his parents live in the area. At the time of the fires that resulted in ferry access being restricted, Tschanz was smuggled through the toxic smoke on a shipping boat with a friend. “It was just to document things and then create a GoFundMe page, and we had a video that would help people that had lost a lot in the community, but then what happened was the beautiful story of the community coming together and forming an organization.” That organization, Tschanz, said is the Chinook Emergency Response Society which is now a national blueprint on how smaller communities can be part of the solution when there is wildfire and they are too remote to access and provide resources and time. This is where the story takes off, according to Tschanz, telling more than just the fires themselves but the aftermath and what happened during that time. article.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
article.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

After removing natural climate fluctuations, researchers confirmed the acceleration with more than 98% statistical confidence.

article.title: [nationalobserver.com] Canada’s climate minister defends record as COP31 opens amid coal dispute
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Canadian Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin defended the government’s climate record before the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, citing methane action, electrification and international climate financing as evidence of Canada’s commitment to its targets. She is attending the conference’s first week, when activists expect other countries to question Canada’s recent policy shifts. The dispute centres on Ottawa’s unfulfilled 2021 pledge to ban thermal-coal exports: an environment commissioner’s report said work was abandoned in 2024 and formally ended in August 2025. Dabrusin said the previous government made the decision and her government is open to next steps. Climate advocates say continued exports undermine Canada’s leadership in the Powering Past Coal Alliance.

Climate funding: Ottawa says it committed to providing $13 billion in climate-related support to developing countries over five years, beginning with an announcement in April 2026 (canada.ca). Methane pledge: Dabrusin plans to co-convene a ministerial meeting with the European Union for the Global Methane Pledge, whose 159 members aim to cut methane emissions by 30% from 2020 levels by 2030 (nationalobserver.com, thestar.com). Fossil fuel concerns: Experts interviewed by Le Devoir and cited in a National Observer report argued that expanding oil and gas production conflicts with Canada’s net-zero goal. The report cited a proposed Pacific Link pipeline with an estimated cost of $35 billion to $45 billion (nationalobserver.com).

Central Chilcotin Rehabilitation Ltd. (CCR) recently received the 2026 Cando (Council for the Advancement of Native Development Officers) Indigenous Private Sector Business Award. The award was presented during the non-profit society’s annual national conference held Oct. 5 to Oct. 8 in Victoria as part of its Economic Developer of the Year Awards. In a news release, CCR CEO and elected councillor of Tŝideldel First Nation Percy Guichon called it a proud moment for CCR and the communities behind it. “We have a lot of damaged forests in our territories, and we’ve worked hard to rehabilitate that land while creating jobs and opportunities for our people,” he stated. “This award recognizes the crews, communities, businesses, and partners who have helped us get this work done.” According to its webpage, CCR was originally formed as a joint venture between the Tŝideldel First Nation and Tl’etinqox Government in the spring of 2017 to address the 100,000 hectares of dead pine left in the Chilcotin region and to rehabilitate those stands into productive forests. In summer 2017, fires amplified the need to address heavily burned forest stands with minimal economic value. Yunesit’in Government joined the joint venture in 2024. Member nations are provided a direct role in forestry projects within their territories while building local skills and business opportunities which Philippe Theriault, General Manager of TŝiDelDel Enterprises, said makes a difference for their communities. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

article.title: [ScienceDaily] A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Researchers at Brown University have overcome a major obstacle to creating ultra-low-power computer chips that could help slash the energy demands of AI. Their breakthrough eliminates a long-standing "dead layer" problem that causes promising materials to stop working when made extremely thin. article.title: [africanews.com] Guinea mining crackdown prompts mass expulsions as workers begin leaving Mali
article.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Hundreds of gold miners expelled from Guinea began leaving an assembly site in Mali by truck and bus on Nov. 11, after Guinea banned clandestine mining in the Siguiri region. Mali said on Nov. 7 that it had received around 160,000 people expelled from Guinea. It also reported six deaths and described the situation as a humanitarian emergency. Guinea’s campaign targets unregulated mining that authorities say damages the environment; the ban took effect Nov. 2. Mali and Burkina Faso are organizing returns, with Burkina Faso’s government preparing an evacuation and repatriation plan for Burkinabe citizens.

article.title: [tsln.com] Cattle specialists urge targeted winter feeding to manage costs
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow. Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs. Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency.
article.summary: Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane
article._excerpt: Cattle advisers and researchers are urging producers to match winter rations to forage quality and herd needs. Drought has tightened forage supplies, and feed is a major operating expense. South Dakota State University research found that limit-fed, energy-dense diets reduced feed use and methane emissions without harming calf growth through weaning, saving about $29 per cow (tsln.com). Kansas State University cow-calf specialist Jason Warner recommends assessing forage and supplementing protein as dormant grasses lose quality. French livestock trainer Guillaume Beaure describes reducing feed waste by closely matching rations to animals’ needs (beefmagazine.com, lafranceagricole.fr). Advisers also recommend checking forage mineral levels because winter hay can pose a risk of magnesium deficiency (tsln.com). Residue quality: Residue baled using the EZBale method measured about 44% total digestible nutrients in the research, compared with 39% for conventionally raked bales; untreated residue alone did not meet pregnant cows’ energy and protein needs (tsln.com). Protein costs: Warner advises comparing supplements by cost per unit of protein. His examples put dried distillers grains at $750 per ton on a 100%-protein basis and wheat middlings at about $1,471 (beefmagazine.com). Mineral checks: Nebraska guidance identifies hay with magnesium levels below 0.15% as low in magnesium. Risk rises when the hay is also low in calcium and high in potassium, which can interfere with magnesium absorption (tsln.com).
article._kite_context: Quote: "Supplying a half to a pound of protein per day in addition to grazing is normally adequate for late-gestation cows." (Jason Warner, Kansas State University cow-calf specialist, BEEF Magazine)

article.title: [The Guardian Global Development] El Niño will increase risk of death in childbirth for millions, say midwives
article.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Effects of extreme weather expected in countries that already have high maternal and newborn death rates

El Niño stokes a higher risk of death in childbirth for millions of women in the world’s harshest crisis zones, midwives have warned.

Converging waves of weather – floods, cyclones and extreme heat – forecast to peak in the coming months will prove fatal for many, especially pregnant women, who face being cut off from hospital when in labour.
